A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-SR research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V2 reports original symbolic-regression experiments across four scientific problems, including comparative results, component ablations and qualitative discovery trajectories.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, ablations, noise tests, perplexity analysis and GPT-4o experiments.

M1.justification: The intended method retains LLM-generated program skeletons, BFGS/Adam parameter fitting, negative-MSE scoring and multi-island experience management. Consolidated pseudocode, revised prompt illustrations and additional backbone evaluations do not establish a changed algorithm. The appendix sampling-formula edit does not establish an implemented procedure change.

E1.justification: The two oscillator tasks, E. coli growth, aluminum stress-strain data and Feynman investigations remain. V3 adds an evaluation scenario with Gaussian-corrupted training observations for Oscillation 2 (Appendix F.1), extending input conditions without adding a scientific domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated NeSymReS and E2E baselines to the original GPlearn, DSR, uDSR and PySR comparisons. NeSymReS excludes the four-input growth task. Appendix F.2 additionally evaluates LMX and adapted FunSearch against LLM-SR on both oscillator tasks, substantially broadening the comparator families.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes reported GPlearn population size from 1,000 to 500, DSR/uDSR batch size from 500 to 512, and PySR from population size 4,000 with up to 100 subpopulations to 15 populations of 33. The PDFs do not establish whether these revisions reflect reruns. New experiments also introduce conditional-perplexity evaluation, four noise levels and controlled LLM comparisons, including GPT-4o at 2,500 iterations.

E4.justification: V3 adds the program-representation ablation, extends prior/program ablations across all four tasks, tests single-island deterministic selection, and examines noise robustness and backbone sensitivity (Appendices E–F). Appendix C adds perplexity-based memorization analysis. Conversely, v2's numerical-differentiation shortcut case is removed from the qualitative appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions report five baseline executions in Appendix A and present point estimates without seed identifiers, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. V3 does not establish increased repetitions or a new uncertainty-reporting practice; its Gaussian-noise standard deviations describe experimental perturbations.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 cells remain unchanged, but new baseline rows and Tables 3–5 substantially expand the results. Cross-task averages are removed, and convergence trajectories are revised (v2 Figure 4; v3 Figure 3). Table 5 reports GPT-4o Oscillation 2 ID/OOD NMSE of 4.27e-10/1.29e-6. On Oscillation 1, GPT-4o has lower OOD error but higher ID error than both earlier backbones.

T1.justification: Appendix B changes the sign of the program-length sampling exponential while retaining its length definition. Section 2.1 also changes the objective's expectation index from candidate programs to data. V3 removes the derivative identity explaining v2's numerical-differentiation shortcut. These are limited mathematical revisions; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient equation discovery using scientific priors and improved OOD generalization remain. V3 makes the four benchmarks designed to prevent recitation an explicit introductory contribution and adds program representation to the components claimed essential for success.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations linking noise resilience to scientific priors and island diversity to avoiding premature convergence, expands the memorization argument using perplexity, and reframes material modeling around empirical discovery. It removes v2's explanation of the numerical-differentiation shortcut, while retaining the general computational-cost and LLM-knowledge limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D add Mixtral hardware details, a ten-parameter limit, numerical sampling-temperature settings, Transformer preprocessing and sampling configurations, and explicit dataset locations and licenses. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. The disclosures are distinct from the revisions to previously stated baseline settings.

R1.justification: The three main related-work strands remain, but v3 adds scientific-agent and recitation references, including Ji et al. (2024) and Wu et al. (2023), and develops explicit distinctions from LMX and FunSearch. It removes the discussion of dimensional-constraint approaches and associated citations such as Tenachi et al. (2023).

P1.justification: V3 extensively condenses and rewrites the methodology, combines the former experimental setup, findings and analysis sections into Section 3, and rewrites the introduction and conclusion. Implementation material is reorganized, and the former qualitative Appendix E becomes Appendix G alongside new analysis sections.

P2.justification: V3 redesigns prompt and trajectory figures, expands oscillator comparison panels, adds Tables 3–5 and new perplexity, ablation and noise displays, and restructures Table 1. Existing appendix equation panels are enlarged and rearranged, and the document adopts the ICLR layout. These changes extend well beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: The added Transformer/LLM comparisons, targeted ablations and noise tests strengthen empirical support, while expanded configuration and data-access information aids reproducibility. These benefits are tempered by removal of the shortcut case and substantial baseline-setting revisions without explaining their relationship to unchanged Table 1 scores. The evidence supports a limited overall improvement.
